Indefinite integrals (antiderivatives)

An antiderivative of f is a function F whose derivative is f. The indefinite integral ∫f(x) dx=F(x)+C represents all of them at once, since adding any constant C does not change the derivative. This calculator integrates term by term using a table of standard rules, shows which rule each term needs, and checks its answer by differentiating it.

Try changing the input

Integrate cos⁡(2x) and then cos⁡(5x): the answer gains a factor 12 or 15 because of the inner linear function — the reverse of the chain rule.

Here u=ax+b is linear. Sums and constant multiples of these are integrated term by term; polynomials in factored form are expanded first.

Worked example

∫(3x2+4cos⁡2x−1x)dx

Step 1 — Term by term

∫3x2 dx=x3,∫4cos⁡2x dx=2sin⁡2x,∫1x dx=ln⁡∣x∣

Step 2 — Combine and add C

x3+2sin⁡2x−ln⁡∣x∣+C

Step 3 — Check

ddx[x3+2sin⁡2x−ln⁡∣x∣]=3x2+4cos⁡2x−1x  ✓

Limitations

  • Only the forms in the table are supported. Integrals that need substitution with a non-linear inner function, integration by parts (such as ∫xsin⁡x dx) or partial fractions are reported as unsupported rather than guessed.
  • Some functions, such as e−x2, have no elementary antiderivative at all; use the definite integral calculator for their numerical values.
  • Every answer is verified by differentiating it and comparing with the integrand at several points.
